notes.meaning: The annual Passover feast and the week-long Festival of Unleavened Bread were drawing near in Jerusalem. These holy days remembered how God freed Israel from slavery in Egypt long ago. By Jesus' day, the people often treated both celebrations as one big festival.

The chief priests and teachers of the law plotted secretly to put Jesus to death. They wanted Him out of the way, but they were terrified of the crowds. Many ordinary people respected Jesus, so an open arrest could start a riot.

Satan entered into Judas Iscariot, who was one of Jesus' twelve chosen apostles. The devil worked through Judas's greed and prompted him to betray his Master. Judas was fully responsible for his choice because he opened his heart to evil.

Judas slipped away to talk with the leading priests and the captains of the temple guard. The rulers needed an insider who knew where Jesus spent quiet hours away from the crowds. Judas offered to help them corner Jesus in private.

The religious leaders were delighted by Judas's offer and promised to pay him silver. Judas agreed to sell out his Teacher for the price of an ordinary servant. Greed had blinded him to the awful evil of what he was doing.

Judas gave his word to hand Jesus over and started looking for the right moment. He needed a time when the crowds were gone so there would be no public outcry. Wicked plots often seek the dark where nobody is watching.

The day came when Jewish law required families to sacrifice the Passover lamb. The lamb's blood had once saved Israel's firstborn sons from death in Egypt. Jesus carefully obeyed God's law as He prepared for His own coming sacrifice.

Jesus chose Peter and John and sent them ahead to get the Passover meal ready. Preparing the feast meant securing an unblemished lamb, bitter herbs, and flat bread made without yeast. Jesus took the lead in preparing this holy evening.

The two disciples asked Jesus where He wanted them to set up the meal. The feast had to be eaten inside the city walls of Jerusalem, but they had no house of their own there. They trusted Jesus to direct their steps.

Jesus told them that as they entered Jerusalem, a man carrying a water jar would meet them. This was an unmistakable sign, because women usually carried water jugs while men carried leather water bags. They were instructed to follow that man to his home.

The disciples were told to ask the master of the house for the guest room where Jesus could eat with His followers. Calling Jesus 'the Teacher' showed that the homeowner likely knew and respected Him. Jesus kept the location private so Judas could not disrupt the meal beforehand.

Jesus promised that the owner would show them a large upstairs room that was already furnished with rugs and couches. The disciples were to complete all the dinner preparations in that room. Everything was ready under God's quiet care.

Peter and John went into the city and found every detail exactly as Jesus had said. They roasted the lamb and set out the herbs, wine, and unleavened bread. Following the Lord's instructions never leads to disappointment.

When twilight arrived, Jesus reclined at the table with His twelve apostles. Following the banquet custom of the day, guests leaned on low couches as they ate together. This quiet dinner brought the disciples together with their Lord for the last time before the cross.

Jesus told His friends how deeply He had longed to share this final Passover with them before His suffering began. He looked forward to this meal because He was about to give His life to redeem the world. His great love for His people carried Him willingly toward death.

Jesus explained that He would not eat the Passover again until its full meaning was fulfilled in the kingdom of God. The old shadow of animal sacrifices was finishing its work. It pointed forward to Christ's great victory and the heavenly feast to come.

Jesus took a cup of wine, thanked God for it, and told the disciples to share it among themselves. A traditional Passover meal included four ceremonial cups of wine, and this was an early cup during the feast. Jesus shared these blessings generously with His followers.

Jesus stated that He would not drink wine again until God's kingdom arrived in its fullness. His earthly life with them was closing, and the cross was only hours away. His words directed their hearts toward the eternal joy waiting ahead.

Jesus took the bread, gave thanks to God, broke it into pieces, and handed it to the disciples. He told them the bread represented His own body, which was given as a sacrifice for their sins. He commanded them to keep repeating this meal in remembrance of Him.

differ.view: Lutherans teach that Christ's literal physical body and blood are truly present in, with, and under the bread and wine.
Reformed Christians teach that Christ's body remains in heaven, but believers truly share in His spiritual presence through faith during the meal.
Baptists generally understand the bread and cup to be symbols that remember Christ's finished work on the cross.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholics believe the bread and wine change completely into Christ's actual body and blood, and that Jesus appointed the apostles as priests to offer this sacrifice in the Mass.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the original text of Luke ended at verse 19a, leaving a shorter account where the cup came before the bread.

notes.meaning: After dinner, Jesus took the cup and declared that it was the new covenant sealed by His poured-out blood. A covenant is a sacred agreement between God and His people. Jesus' death established God's promise to wipe away sin and give believers new life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: A number of scholars view this verse as part of a later addition because certain early manuscripts leave out verses 19b–20 entirely and describe only one cup before the bread.

notes.meaning: Jesus pointed out that the hand of His betrayer was resting right beside His on the table. Eating from the same dish was an ancient sign of close friendship and mutual trust. Betraying someone after sharing a table with them showed the coldest kind of treachery.

Jesus declared that He was going to the cross just as God had planned before time began. Yet God's sovereign plan did not excuse the traitor, and terrible judgment awaited the man who betrayed Him. God uses even wicked actions for good, but wrongdoers remain guilty for their sins.

The apostles were stunned and began asking one another which of them could do something so awful. None of them suspected Judas, because he had hidden his evil heart behind an outwardly faithful life. We must look honestly at our own hearts rather than assuming we could never fall.

A sharp argument broke out among the disciples about which of them was considered the greatest. Even at this holy meal and right before Jesus died, human pride and ambition caused division. Christ's followers are called to put away rivalry and seek humble service instead.
